3 John 1.summary: Third John is a short, personal letter from a man who calls himself ‘the elder’ to a Christian named Gaius, whom he loves ‘in truth.’ The elder opens with a prayer that all may go well with Gaius and that he may be in good health, just as it is going well with his soul. He rejoices because traveling believers have come and reported that Gaius is walking in the truth, and he says he has no greater joy than hearing that his ‘children’ are walking in the truth. He praises Gaius for acting faithfully toward the ‘brothers,’ even though they were strangers to him. These traveling Christians told the church about Gaius’s love. The elder asks him to continue sending them on their way ‘in a manner worthy of God,’ because they went out ‘for the sake of the name,’ taking nothing from the Gentiles, and so believers should support such people and become ‘fellow workers for the truth.’ He then reports a problem. He has written something to the church, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, does not acknowledge the elder’s authority. The elder says that if he comes he will bring up what Diotrephes is doing: spreading malicious nonsense against ‘us,’ refusing to welcome the brothers, stopping those who want to welcome them, and putting them out of the church. The elder urges Gaius not to imitate evil but good, because whoever does good is from God and whoever does evil has not seen God. He commends a man named Demetrius, who has a good testimony from everyone and from the truth itself, and the elder adds his own testimony. He closes by saying he had much more to write but would rather talk face to face, hopes to visit soon, and sends greetings of peace from the friends with a request that Gaius greet the friends by name.
3 John 1.whereWeAre:
Early Christians moved around the Roman Empire to preach and teach. Jesus had sent out disciples dependent on hospitality (Matthew 10:9-14), and New Testament letters repeatedly urge believers to show hospitality (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2; 1 Peter 4:9).

Ancient writers often describe public inns as rough, unsafe, or morally disreputable, so travelers who could rely on a host’s home had a great advantage. For Christians, a network of believers’ homes served this purpose.

Churches in the first century commonly met in private homes (Romans 16:5; Colossians 4:15; Philemon 1:2). A host had considerable influence, and decisions about who was welcomed could be made by the person who controlled the house or the meeting. This is a probable background to Diotrephes’s ability to refuse and expel, though the letter does not describe how he held his position.

The Didache, an early Christian manual probably from the late first or early second century, instructs churches to welcome traveling apostles and prophets, limits their stay to a short period, and warns against those who ask for money or exploit hospitality (Didache 11–12). It shows that hospitality toward traveling teachers needed both generosity and discernment. It does not mention Diotrephes or this letter.

Papias’s preface, as read by Eusebius (Church History 3.39), mentions both the apostle John and an ‘elder John,’ and Eusebius takes these to be two different people. Eusebius lists 2 and 3 John among the books some disputed (3.25), and reports that Origen said the second and third letters might not be accepted by all as genuine (6.25). The letters were short and less widely quoted than 1 John, which probably explains why they were slower to be widely recognized.

The second letter of John (2 John 1:10-11) tells readers not to receive those who do not bring the true teaching of Christ. Whether the dispute with Diotrephes relates to a conflict over teaching or to personal rivalry is unknown. Because traveling believers relied on local hosts, Diotrephes’s refusal to welcome them would have cut off their ministry in his church and also cut off the elder’s influence there. Gaius’s hospitality kept the network of care working. The letter’s request to continue helping the travelers, together with its commendation of Demetrius, fit this setting of mutual support among connected churches.

keyFigures.name: The elder (the author)
keyFigures.role: He writes to commend Gaius, warn about Diotrephes, recommend Demetrius, and announce a possible visit. He shows pastoral concern that reaches Gaius and a church through letters and messengers.

keyFigures.name: Gaius
keyFigures.role: He is praised for faithfulness and asked to continue helping the travelers, to avoid imitating evil, and is told of Demetrius’s good testimony. He is the example of practical hospitality and truth lived out.

keyFigures.name: The ‘brothers’ (the traveling Christians)
keyFigures.role: They are the recipients of Gaius’s hospitality and the people Diotrephes refuses to welcome. They represent the mission work that relied on the support of local believers.

keyFigures.name: The church
keyFigures.role: It hears the report about Gaius and is the setting of Diotrephes’s actions. It shows that early churches were connected by traveling believers and letters.

keyFigures.name: Diotrephes
keyFigures.role: He rejects the elder’s authority, spreads malicious accusations, refuses to welcome the brothers, and expels those who do. He is the negative example of pride and abuse of influence.

keyFigures.name: Demetrius
keyFigures.role: He is recommended to Gaius. He is the positive example, in contrast with Diotrephes.

keyFigures.name: ‘My children’
keyFigures.role: The elder’s greatest joy is to hear that they walk in the truth. It shows his fatherly care for them.

keyFigures.name: ‘The Gentiles’ (non-believers)
keyFigures.role: They are mentioned in explaining why the travelers need the support of believers. It clarifies why local believers are the travelers’ providers.

keyFigures.name: ‘The friends’
keyFigures.role: They exchange greetings. It shows the personal ties among the believers.

keyFigures.name: God and ‘the name’ (Christ)
keyFigures.role: They are the basis of the elder’s instructions. The letter’s ethics rest on belonging to God.

keyFigures.name: John the apostle / ‘John the elder’
keyFigures.role: They are not characters in the letter. Their mention reflects an unresolved discussion about authorship.

keyThemes.explanation:
The elder rejoices that Gaius ‘is walking in the truth’ and that his children walk in truth, and he says Demetrius has a testimony from the truth itself.

The letter links sound belief with a life of love and integrity.

keyThemes.theme: Hospitality as partnership in gospel work
keyThemes.explanation:
Gaius is praised for supporting traveling believers, and the elder says that by doing so believers become ‘fellow workers for the truth.’

Practical help for those serving Christ is presented as real participation in their work.

Diotrephes ‘likes to put himself first,’ rejects the elder, slanders others, and blocks and expels those who would show hospitality.

The text warns against self-promotion and control in leadership.

Gaius is told to imitate what is good, since ‘whoever does good is from God; whoever does evil has not seen God.’ Demetrius is an example of a good testimony.

Readers are encouraged to follow good examples and to evaluate leaders by their conduct.

The elder prays for Gaius’s health, calls him beloved, hopes to talk face to face, and sends greetings by name.

The text values personal presence and warmth alongside doctrinal and practical guidance.
